In fairness, and to the extent that Canadians can expect the income tax system to be fair, the child care provision should take into consideration the actual problems encountered by working parents in Canada today.
Let me deal with the proposal contained in the motion. By way of preliminary remarks I should make it clear that the motion is merely a request that the government consider the proposal. The words used are not carved in stone and may not fit exactly with the language now used in Section 63 of the Income Tax Act. I sincerely hope any discrepancies that arise from the letter of the words used will not be used to defeat the spirit and intent of the proposal.
The proposed provision would allow either a mother or a father to claim, by way of deduction on her or his income tax, a specified per diem child care allowance, I have suggested $10 per day for each child under 12 years of age. This claim could be made only when two conditions are met: First, and foremost, the child would have to be given care and supervision by an adult person other than the parent during the day when the parent or parents were at work. That includes single parents; second, the parent claiming the allowance would have to be working and, if that parent had a spouse, the spouse would also have to be working or, alternatively, incapable of caring for the child.
I should point out that if the allowance was claimed for 250 working days, the total would approximate the married exemption of $2,500. By this proposal the requirement which permits the taxpayer to claim the per diem child care allowance has been reduced to two simple conditions. I would ask why? It is clear, when you examine the facts, that a working parent or parents cannot care for a child under 12 years of age and must
Income Tax Act
provide for some kind of day or custodial care. Second, there must be a financial cost involved in providing day or custodial care when that care is provided by a person other than the parent, whether that person receives cash or some other benefit.
I am well aware the proposal does not require a specified cash payment to the person who provides the child care. Let me explain why. Quite often, the person best able to provide day or custodial care to the children of working parents is the mother of one of the parents. I am sure almost everyone is aware of a situation in which the grandmother or grandparents provide care to grandchildren while the parents work. Whether the grandsparents make a financial charge or whether some other benefit is provided should be a private, family matter. The point is that custodial care is being provided to permit a single parent or both parents to work and earn income which is then taxed to the full extent permitted by law.
There are many examples in the Income Tax Act where an allowance is provided that is not dependent upon the actual dollars expended. The personal exemption which is $2,890 for 1980, the married exemption which is $2,530 and the dependent child exemption which is $540 are all examples of allowances not related to actual expenditures.
Another relevant example is the employment expense deduction which presupposes that a working person must incur certain expenses related to employment like clothes, equipment and similar items. This allowance is fixed at 3 per cent of employment earnings to a maximum of $500.
Another clear example is the $100 deduction for charitable contributions described in the income tax form as the "standard deduction". Again, the law presupposes actual expenses for medical care and charities of at least $100 per year and does not require an accounting below that level.
My question, then, is simply this: is it not equally fair to presuppose or assume for purposes of the Income Tax Act that single or working parents who arrange to have their children cared for while working incurs extra expenses? Whether those expenses should be fixed at an allowance equal to $10 per day or should be subject to some over-all total maximum like $4,000, I would not want to argue. I recognize the difficulty in establishing a fair amount. But I will argue most vehemently, and in principle, that there should be a child care allowance of some kind for single and working parents.
Let me point out that a single parent or working parents would not have the benefit of the married exemption which is $2,530 for 1980. There may be a possibility of a claim for the equivalent to the married exemption provided under the Income Tax Act, but that would depend on special circumstances. Certainly, it would be a simple matter to ensure that a taxpayer could not claim both a married or equivalent exemption and a child care allowance. I should also say that I do not think the matter is affected by the child tax credit which applies universally.
My point, regardless, is this very simple one. The Income Tax Act should recognize the fact that single and working

March 23, 1981
Income Tax Act
parents incur child care expenses and should be provided some additional child care allowance based on this fact.
Let us consider what is involved in the child care provisions of the Income Tax Act. When they were initially enacted, it was recognized that there was a certain difficulty in establishing a reasonable amount to be permitted for child care expenses. Many of the promoters of the provisions enacted in the act-I believe, in the early 1970s-felt they provided a motive for women to return to the work force, knowing that they would incur expenses for child care, and that their effective incomes would be reduced by the cost of those expenses.
It may be that in this day and age the government does not want to encourage women to return to the work force. But in the 1980s I think it is accepted by most people that married women, whether or not they have children, have a right in our society to join the work force if that is their desire. I do not think that depriving those women, or men, of an adequate child care allowance should be used as a deterrent to keep those people out of the work force.
The Income Tax Act is difficult in terms of determining its philosophy. But to the extent there is a philosophy behind it, it is certainly that it distinguished between those costs which are part of the cost of living as opposed to those costs which are part of the cost of earning a living. I do not think any authority on income tax law in Canada or in the United States would disagree that child care expenses are very much a part of the cost of earning a living when they are incurred in order to allow the person in question to keep working or to join the work force.
Therefore I think, in terms of the philosophy involved in the Income Tax Act that should be applied to this provision, it is clear that the government, through the instrumentation of the Income Tax Act, should recognize the fact that child care expenses are very much a part of the cost of earning a living for people who would not otherwise incur those costs; that is, they would not incur those costs unless they were in the work force.
As I have said, I do not think it is fair to take advantage of those people, in terms of deterring them from entering the work force or from staying in the work force by unfair provisions respecting deductions for child care costs. It is simply not fair, as is the present case, to take advantage of those persons who incur child care costs having regard to the reluctance of persons who care for children in those circumstances, to require the amounts paid to them to be recorded. Provisions in the Income Tax Act now require as a condition of claiming child care costs, that the person obtain a receipt, which receipt must contain the social insurance number of the person who receive the child care payments. Many persons who provide these services by way of baby sitting or custodial day care do not want to become involved with the income tax system to the extent of disclosing the existence of these payments. This works a hardship on many people across the land. That is one other reason for permitting a non-accountable allowance in respect of child care, bearing in mind that
somewhere down the line the cost of child care must be borne by the working parent.
At the same time, the provisions of the Income Tax Act are very clear in respect of the responsibility of recipients of any payments to report the same to the Income Tax Department. However, we should not require those parents who must provide custodial day care for their children in order to permit them to work to be policemen for the Income Tax Department.
One final point which has been made time and time again is that the current provisions of Section 63 of the Income Tax Act discriminate against males, that is, working fathers who are required to care for their children. They are subjected, as I have indicated, to more onerous provisions than working mothers. We do not have too many examples these days where male persons are subject to discrimination under the law. I certainly do not think males across Canada need an advocate in me or any other member of the House of Commons. However, this is one area in which sex discrimination rears its ugly head and is an evil in itself, an intrinsic evil, whether it is applied to men or women. That is one more reason for asking the government to look at this motion, to review the provision of the Income Tax Act respecting child care expenses and to come up with some method, some technique, that will be fair in its application, and will not place such a burden on the working parents of Canada.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to have the opportunity to participate in this debate. I think the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) deserves to be congratulated for his proposal, for taking the time to organize his material and for making such a good presentation. I notice that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has been in the chamber for the last 20 minutes. It is unfortunate he has not been paying attention. If anyone should pay attention, it should be the minister. He missed a very good opportunity to hear some ideas on this subject so ably put forward by the hon. member for Halifax West. The minister is responsible for the Income Tax Act which should not only be used by the Department of National Revenue for the collection of taxes but to encourage people to be productive. Productive people pay more taxes and the measures outlined by the hon. member would help to bring this about.
I noticed that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) paid close attention to the speech, so I hope he can prevail upon the minister to adopt some of the points made by my colleague.
The motion contains many reasonable and sensible provisions. Parents should only be able to claim if both work or in the event of a single parent. A deduction could be claimed for children 12 years of age or under. This strikes me as entirely reasonable. The motion provides that the government "should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act to
March 23, 1981

permit the mother or father of one or more children to deduct $10 per day as a child care allowance-
The hon. member is asking that the House refer this matter to the appropriate committee; that is, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I have had an opportunity to sit on this committee and know it to be very busy and effective. I hope the government will refer the motion to the committee.
I live on a farm in a very sparsely populated part of the country so I know some of the problems parents encounter when trying to find people to care for their children while they are away at work. People who live in cities and in the larger centres have easier access to day care, or other good care for their children while they work. This is next to impossible to find in the country where just not enough people live close enough together to provide such professional services.
It seems to me when money is allocated for day care by the provinces it inevitably goes to the larger centres where there is enough population to justify the centres. 1 think that is rather unfair to the people who live in these sparsely populated areas. The motion would go a long way toward alleviating the inequalities presently in the system. It certainly makes sense to me.
There is other evidence of the well-reasoned thought that has gone into the presentation of this motion. Ten dollars per day is not a large amount and the program would not be expensive to administer. It could be done on the basis of the T-4 tax slip which is sent to everyone who pays tax. It would be a simple matter to use that slip as a means of establishing the number of days worked by the parent.
One of the great shortcomings of the Income Tax Act is that it is difficult to understand and complicated to administer. The hon. member for Halifax West referred to Section 63 of the Income Tax Act, but I am afraid that unless one was paying very close attention to what he said one would find it difficult to understand.
This motion, however, is simple and straightforward and it would let people know where they stand with the tax department at the end of the year. It would give them the incentive to find extra work in order to meet their obligations. The more people who work in this country, the greater will our production be, and the Minister of Finance should consider that.
Children are a very important resource of this country and it is important that they be looked after properly. This motion would be an incentive to parents to meet their obligations toward their children.
It would be appropriate for the finance committee to consider the real cost. The Department of National Revenue could simply look at this, take a figure out of the air, say that at present there is a $1,000 exemption for a child and that, if the figures proposed in the motion were used, one could end up witlj a tax deduction of some $2,500, the difference being $1,500 as an exemption.
If additional jobs were created there would be more money in the economy. The result would be an increase in government
Income Tax Act
revenues. I would be interested in having some of the officials from the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Finance appear before the finance committee and go over the net cost of the proposal, which I suspect would turn out to be less than we expect.
A jurisdictional problem is also involved in that day care is a provincial matter and the motion deals with a federal matter. If this proposal or something similar were adopted, the full cost could be borne by the federal government, but I feel the provinces should be willing to shoulder some of the cost of the lost revenue the federal government would suffer.
This is an excellent suggestion, mr. Speaker, and I congratulate the hon. member for Halifax West for doing his homework and for presenting such a well-reasoned argument. I hope the matter will be referred to the appropriate committee so it can be examined to find out the net cost and the benefit to the country, especially to the children. As we all know they are this country's most valuable resource.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance);
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to pick up on what the hon. member for Portage-Mar-quette (Mr. Mayer) has just mentioned with regard to the federal-provincial aspects of this motion. They are very important and we have seen some difficulties with respect to them. I agree wholeheartedly with him that this subject, if it were to be adopted at some point by the federal government as an approach to resolving the great financial difficulties many of our citizens face in respect of day care expenses, would have to be very carefully worked out with the provincial governments.
When the federal government has brought forward programs in the past which transfer moneys to individuals or to the provinces to help defray the costs of programs and areas of responsibility, provincial in nature, in many cases-and I am not saying that as an unequivocal statement-we have seen that the provinces have tended financially to move out from that area to an extent closely corresponding to the amount by which the federal government has moved in. As a result, the kinds of programs in the area of day care, for example, could very well leave the individuals no better off than they are right now, but could leave the federal treasury worse off, and provincial treasuries better off. I would think that would be an area to be very carefully explored with the provinces so that we do not run into the kind of problem the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has related to us concerning medicare, or the kinds of problems we are facing now in the area of post-secondary education. In some cases we find that the federal contribution to post-secondary education in certain provinces exceeds 100 per cent of the cost of post-secondary education, when the original intent was to have a program in which the federal government would participate with the provinces to defray part of the costs, in some cases 50 per cent in a shared arrangement between federal and provincial governments.

March 23. 1981
Income Tax Act
I would not want to see a program in which the federal government enriched its tax expenditures to assist all citizens in day care expenses, with the result that provincial goven-ments pulled back their existing funding of day care, such that individuals would be no better off after the introduction of new tax expenditure than they are now. That is a very serious problem and one which the newly established parliamentary task force to look into the question of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, could very well explore.
All Canadians would benefit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend who is making comments on the other side of the House.
Something which I will certainly recommend, and I hope he will support and recommend along with me, is that the newly formed federal-provincial task force look not only at this kind of thing, in addition to the existing federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, but also at other potential areas, including the kinds of relationships and arrangements we should put into place between the federal government and the provincial governments to ensure that when an increase in funding comes from one level of government, be it the provincial or the federal government, the individuals to whom the program is intended to benefit are the beneficiaries and not one or other levels of government.
With that said, I would like to turn my attention now specifically to the motion. This motion relates to income tax deductions for child care expenses. It deals with two separate issues. The first calls for an increase in the amount of allowable child care expenses that may be deducted, and I will return to this question shortly. The other issue, which is a far more complex one, and one which hon. members opposite have spent a great deal of time on, raises the basic principle of this tax provision and asks the fundamental question: What does this particular tax provision seek to achieve?
It is argued that this is a discriminatory provision in our tax law. Indeed, that was the finding recently of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, after examining the complaints of male taxpayers that they did not enjoy equal treatment to that accorded to women by this section of the Income Tax Act.
Briefly, the point of contention lies in the fact that the deduction for child care expenses is available to women with no qualifying restrictions as to their marital status or circumstances within that marriage, but it is available to men only in limited circumstances.
A mother who has a paid job or operates a self-employed business may claim the expense deduction regardless of whether she is a single mother, or whether she has a husband who also works to support the family, or whether, indeed, her husband stays home and acts as a house-husband, so to speak.
But a man, to qualify for the deduction, must be a single or a separated parent or, if he is married, his wife must be unable through illness or as the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) indicated through incarceration to care for their children. In other words, a father will be allowed to deduct
child care expenses only in circumstances where he has to seek outside help in caring for his children while he works.
Having said that, I think it must be clear, however, that in actual practice the great majority of women who claim the child care expenses as tax deduction need the income that comes from their job. I do not have to cite statistics to demonstrate the importance of money earned by women in the labour force toward supporting the family budget. Yet the fact remains that the deduction is available to men only in certain circumstances, while it is generally available to women.
Following the decision last fall by the Human Rights Commission, the Commissioner, Gordon Fairweather, said recently that this is discrimination and that it can be changed only by Parliament.
If we conclude that discrimination exists, however, it does not automatically follow that it should be removed. The Income Tax Act discriminates, and deliberately so, in other ways as well. Are younger people improperly discriminated against, for example, by the special deduction for the elderly? Or consider the proposed charter of human rights which stipulates that special treatment in the form of affirmative action programs to improve the position of certain groups does not constitute a breach of the rule against discrimination, found in that charter. So in the case before us, as in other areas, we have to consider carefully whether the discriminatory treatment is justified.
The deduction for child care expenses in the Income Tax Act was introduced in 1972, as part of the major tax reform being introduced at that time. Its preferential treatment for women has been no secret over the years since then. Yet no minister of finance during that period, including the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) in the previous government, has felt it appropriate to change that provision.
In fact, in 1976, in the wake of the 1975 International Year of the Woman, the maximum deduction allowable under the act for child care expenses was doubled. Why should Parliament have enacted this sort of discrimination in 1971 and confirmed it five years later?
The rationale for the initial measure as part of Tax Reform was stated in 1969 in the government's white paper on tax Reform, which said:
This new plan is intended primarily to benefit mothers who need to work to support their families, and would be in addition to the normal exemption for children.
During the International Year of the Woman there was a very clear need identified for measures expressly designed to alleviate the plight of women in the work force. Probably the chief discrimination against women in the work force was the fact that they were generally paid less than men-a situation which continues to exist, unfortunately, to this day. Making the child care expense deduction generally available to women was seen as one way by which the state could redress some of these grievances.
In addition is the fact that, in spite of changing values, women are still traditionally held responsible for the care and
March 23, 1981

nurture of children. I think that is further explanation of why the allowance is generally available to women, but available to men only in most circumstances in which the children's mother is not available to help care for them.
I should note an exception to that last generalization. In order to claim the expense deduction, a man who is separated from his wife must have a legal separation order or written agreement. If he has been deserted by his wife without the legal formalities he does not qualify for the deduction, unless his separation is confirmed by court order. This tax rule exists purely for administrative reasons; how else could one verify separation or marriage breakdown. This is one of the particular problems raised by the Human Rights Commission, and the government will certainly give careful study to that problem.
Ever since the deduction for child care expenses went into effect in 1972 it has been criticized as an example of sexism, or perhaps I should say reverse sexism. There are strongly opposing viewpoints and basic philosophies behind both sides of the argument.
One view sees the child care expenses as a personal expense that arises as a consequence of the mother's discretionary decision to work outside the home. It is her traditional responsibility to care for the children, the argument goes, and if she decides to go out to work, that is her decision made in the knowledge that child care costs will have to be paid. Since there are already tax benefits accruing to a couple where both partners are working, the public should not be expected to provide what is, in effect, a further subsidy through allowing deduction of the child care expenses.
The other contrasting viewpoint, one that I tend to share, sees child care as a shared responsibility and concern of the whole society, and one which should therefore be supported out of the public treasury. It follows from this argument that where a taxpayer must pay for child care in order to work, this should be considered a real expense of earning income and should be fully deductible. I think that is the spirit of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Halifax West.
Before concluding, I should refer to the other aspect of this notice of motion dealing with the ceiling on child care expenses that may be deducted. The present limits are $30 a week, and $1,000 per year for each child under the age of 14, with a maximum deduction of $4,000 in the year. There is a further stipulation that the deduction may not exceed two thirds of the taxpayer's earned income in the year.
As I said earlier, those maximum deduction levels were set in the 1976 budget, which doubled the previous limits established in 1972. This motion proposes a deduction of $10 a day for children under 12 years of age. Assuming a five-day week, that means $50 a week, or an increase of 66 per cent in the present level. Obviously a change like that would involve a considerable cost to the treasury, not to mention the much larger charge on the treasury if the deduction were made
Income Tax Act
generally available to men. Such a change would have to be considered in the context of other tax changes in a budget.
One point we should bear in mind is that child care expenses are not the only kind of child raising costs for which our tax laws try to provide. There is the basic personal exemption for dependant children, for example, and the child tax credit which is designed to provide help where it is most needed, in low and lower middle-income families. Both these provisions are indexed to reflect inflation. There are other federal programs, including family allowances, which also have to be taken into consideration when we look at this proposal to change the tax deduction for child care expenditures. Furthermore, in our federal system we cannot ignore the various social services to families provided by the provinces which have the main authority in this field.
Since the decision of the Human Rights Commission, studies have been going ahead in the Department of Finance into the possibility of restructuring the existing resources being allocated to child care, to see whether they could be more efficiently applied to achieve the goals we seek. I should add that in his budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) clearly indicated he is going to undertake a major review of tax expenditures in the tax system. I can indicate to the House that this is one of the areas the department is now considering for modification.
In conclusion, what is being proposed here involves a substantial increase in our so-called tax expenditures. These are not the normal cash expenditures, but they have every bit as much impact on our federal deficit. This motion also proposes a fundamental shift in the policy underlying this deduction which was originally intended to help redress the inferior economic position of women in the labour market. I do not think anyone would argue that it does not constitute special treatment for women-call it discrimination if you wish. Hon. members will have to make their own judgments as to whether that special treatment is justified.

Mr. Speaker, we agree that the present tax deduction of $1,000 per child per year is far from adequate. In some cases, this means only one sixth of the child care expense of a family is returned through the deduction. We also agree there should be no sex discrimination and that either a father or mother should be eligible for child care deductions, just as either a father or mother might remain in the home to care for a child.
I commend the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) on some aspects of this resolution. However, I cannot agree that an increased tax deduction which allows $10 per day for child care costs will solve the problem of affordable day care for most parents with average and low incomes in Canada. If we accept this plan, my fear is we would merely be continuing present inequities. Only the very rich and the very poor can afford day care in Canada today. The rich can pay directly and the poor resort to welfare subsidy.
What we need in Canada is a universal form of affordable child care. We must have a government policy which makes
8534

March 23, 1981
Income Tax Act
dependable, accessible and affordable child care a must for any Canadian family that needs it. I agree this is particularly important in rural areas of Canada where there is now really no provision for child care services and cost subsidies.
However, to achieve this goal, if we are trying to do it through the tax system, surely the Income Tax Act must be changed to add a child care tax credit. A tax credit would help pay the cost of child care for persons who do not now earn enough to pay income tax. Many of these are working poor, people with very low incomes. Also, there are those who are not working, in addition to some mothers on their own who need day care service.
This bill raises the whole question of the need for a universal child care program throughout Canada. With 44.5 per cent of Canadian mothers in the work force, there are some 721,000 children under the age of six who have working mothers. Very few of these families, about 12 per cent of them, are able to put children into government-approved day care spaces. In the ten years before 1979 the number of working women increased by 62 per cent. We know this trend is here to stay.
There are many points I would like to raise in support of much more active federal leadership to ensure a universal and affordable child care program in Canada. We all agree with the National Action Commission for the International Year of the Child that children are our greatest resource and must be given the first priority in our various policies.
Family structures in Canada are changing. Child care needs are very great. Child care, and I use that term rather than day care because it has a different connotation, must be flexible, meeting the child's development needs as well as the needs of the family as a whole.
It is also important, since the cost of living is so high, particularly the cost of housing and mortgages today, that in many cases both spouses must work. There must be two breadwinners in the family in order to meet survival costs. This means many couples are putting off having a family, and affordable day care would be a great help to them.
Single-parent families also are increasing at a phenomenal rate. Single parents must be assured of stable, high standard care for their children if they are to seek work and, as I said earlier, many single parents must have the choice to remain at home and care for their children, if that is best for them. We must not force single parents, particularly, into the work force if that is not best for them and their child, but we must have adequate flexible day care in any case.
We in this party feel that the federal government must be much more actively involved in the development of a universal child care policy. We must have federal standards that apply in all provinces, there must be fair financial arrangements involving a fair contribution for those who can afford it, and tax credits or deductions certainly would help in that way.
There also must be, of course, a major contribution from the provinces which carry the main responsibility for day care.
This means funding in advance for operating costs, because they have to keep the doors open and pay the overhead. The federal government should certainly be contributing to start-up and capital costs; such incentives are needed to develop new day care centres but were refused by the responsible minister. The federal government should also be sharing subsidy costs, which it does now to some degree through the Canada Assistance Plan, but this is far from universal. It is very important there be an integrated, shared funding policy with up-front moneys to cover the operating costs for day care centres.
Many people, Mr. Speaker, feel that a child care centre should be an adjunct to neighbourhood schools, and I favour this idea. There are many schools where classrooms are becoming available and, with the help of federal funds, these should be converted to good child care centres operated close to home for mothers where the older children are in the regular school program.
It is estimated there are over one million children between the ages of seven and 12, the so-called latch-key children, who go home to empty houses because their parents work, or the single parent works, and they do not have adequate care for this age group. We need after-school care, summer programs, flexible programs that will include care for infants, perhaps with more homemakers going into the home; and we need registered family day care homes, satellite programs connected to neighbourhood day care centres.
We also need accessible, flexible day care in the workplace where this is the best practical arrangement for the parent and child. I am pleased to say a very active day care committee has been working here on Parliament Hill over the past year to establish a model day care centre, demonstrating the need for workers, not Members of Parliament necessarily, but workers on the Hill to have good day care in the workplace. We appreciate the support Madam Speaker has provided to this movement and hope to have the centre open by next September. I am pleased to hear recently that a federal department, I believe the Treasury Board, is considering implementing a pilot project of this kind.
When we talk about financing our day care centres, it is most important also that we remember there must be adequate, well paid staff for this most important service. For too long I think the attitude of people has been that child care is something that can be done by anyone; why do women, who have been in the home anyway, need to get paid adequate wages, they can go and be a supervisor in a day care centre- at terribly low wages. This is not a part-time job for so-called housewives, and this is an attitude that needs to be changed. There must be adequate funding and staffing at decent union rates of pay for day care supervisors.
I would also like to say, Mr. Speaker, that decent universal child care is far too important a subject to be considered as a result of a private member's bill, with all due respect to the member who presented this resolution. I urge that this be a major topic of debate in the House. The present health, welfare and social affairs committee has been studying the report called "For Canada's Children: National Agenda for
March 23, 1981

Action". This report was presented by the Canadian Commission for the International Year of the Child in 1979, Mr. Speaker. Only now are we getting to this report, and I am ashamed to say that many members on that committee have not shown a great deal of interest in Canada's children and have not been as active as I hoped they would be on this very important issue. I hope this matter will come back to the House for a very serious debate. There is nothing more important than Canada's children and the future of our country depends on adequate care in the home where parents who want to can care for their children, or there should be adequate universal day care available.
In conclusion, I would like to quote excerpts from this report. These are points which I believe are relevant to the debate on this resolution and on which we in this party agree completely. On page 27 it states:
Children have not had equal access to care the way they have had to education.
Child care encompasses a wide range of alternatives to help children develop and flourish as human beings.
Only the very poor and the very rich have access to many of these alternatives.
The major problems in the provision of accessible, available and affordable day care in Canada are cost, jurisdiction and attitude. Although child care is a provincial responsibility, the federal government could participate to a much greater degree and relieve some of the funding problems.
With working parents now the norm, the need for child care programs is more acute than ever. It is unrealistic to expect parents to shoulder the full financial cost of raising the next generation.
Parents who stay at home should have the support they need to best fulfil their caring role.
And finally, Mr. Speaker:
Since healthy, well cared for children are a joy and an asset to their society, the care and well-being of our children should be a responsibility and a trust shared by society as a whole.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words on this important motion that the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) has put before the House. I think it is a very important motion and I hope the government will take notice of it. He brought out a very important point to which he did not address himself, but I think we will have to over the next few years; that is the preservation of the family unit.
Do we as citizens want to simply work, earn a good living, and look after ourselves, or are we going to look beyond ourselves to the question of why we are here and what this is all about? It looks to me like the preservation of the family unit is in reality what we should be looking for in this coming age.
The hon. member brought to our attention the present limitations on parents, whether they be single-parent families or whether both parents work. However, there are severe limitations placed on people who have to work and have to put their children into day care centres for one reason or the other. Because the time is short, I would like to bring to the attention
Adjournment Debate
of the House that a number of years ago as a project coordinator for a building project I spent many hours studying day care centres. Most highrise office buildings are well behind in development for the future.
Do I have more time, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: AIRPORTS-INCREASE IN PASSENGER TRAFFIC AT MALTON, EDMONTON AND CALGARY
AIRPORTS-INCREASE IN PASSENGER TRAFFIC AT MALTON, EDMONTON AND CALGARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Mirabel is a name that conjures up grandiose projects, projects that were meant to make of that spot the largest port of entry into North America! But Mirabel is also an expropriated community of Canadians who were asked to forget the dreams and aspirations that are typical of all members of rural communities. Mirabel is a white elephant. Mirabel, finally, is a ten-year-old issue that would appear to be so complex that each study leads our civil servants to recommend that a further study be made of it in greater detail. And so, year after year, pressing decisions are put off pending the findings of studies that are under way. So much time is spent on those precious studies that I have come to the sad conclusion that what findings are produced are always obsolete and, as time lost breeds new problems, we find ourselves with even more problems to solve. In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, everybody is waiting for the decisions the ministers in charge should be making. The land owners who were expropriated are waiting, as is the whole population of the area and the province of Quebec, because the economic future of Quebec is at stake. I am waiting, and I am sure several hon. members are waiting too. Those the minister responsible considers as Mirabel die-

March 23, 1981
8536______________________________________
Adjournment Debate hards are waiting. In short, everybody is waiting and that is the irony of the situation. Also, everybody knows what should be done. I do not deny the complexity of the problem, and I respect the minister responsible who insists on playing it safe to avoid mistakes at all costs. However, how many more years should we continue waiting? And what price will we have to pay for this prudence which borders on paranoia?
There are two main aspects to this issue. On the one hand, the management of the adjacent lands, and on the other the future of Mirabel airport. As to the first element, I am very pleased with the decision which the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) announced recently to establish a new Crown corporation. However, the future of the airport itself is still in doubt, and this uncertainty is not without adverse consequences on the Quebec economy. Since the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is not present, I should like to direct a series of questions to his parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael), and to avoid all possible misunderstanding, I must advise him that although I have read the Speech from the Throne very attentively, as the Minister of Transport had suggested on December 2,1 have been unable to find any answers to my questions. First of all, what progress in their study have the officials of the Department of Transport made who, after ten years, are still unable to provide us with any additional information on this?
Second, did the parliamentary secretary read the article by Michel Gratton published in the newspaper Le Droit last December 1 ? Can he confirm the increase in passenger traffic at Malton airport, 14 per cent last year, at Edmonton airport with 21 per cent and at Calgary which beat all records with a rise of 23.3 per cent? And can he explain why Mirabel did so poorly, with an increase of 3 per cent? Can he also tell us what steps the Minister of Transport intends to take to turn Mirabel into a money-making venture?
Third, has the Minister of Transport been made aware of the resolution adopted by the Mirabel municipal council on February 3 in which they ask him to authorize the transfer of flights from Dorval to Mirabel? One excerpt from that resolution which I fully endorse is most revealing and deserves to be quoted:
Whereas Mirabel airport has physical and operational features which are unique in North America and in the world because of the particularities of its adjacent territory, because there is no curfew, and because it has the world's most modern cargo and passenger-handling facilities which give it a lead in the operation and the industrial development to which it aspires;
Finally, and it is always the same question every day, when, when, and again when will the minister once and for all take the required decisions? Not only has the time come, we are already late as it is. In my opinion we must act right now. I am convinced that the decision to build that airport in the early seventies was sound. The mistake has been to delay until tomorrow what ought to and could be done today. It is a
complex matter, I admit that, however its characteristic complexity does not justify all that wasted time.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-INCREASE IN PASSENGER TRAFFIC AT MALTON, EDMONTON AND CALGARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Argen-teuil has raised the issue of growing passenger traffic at the Toronto, Edmonton and Calgary airports as well as the question of the measures which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) intends to take to make Mirabel airport more profitable. The increase in passenger traffic at the Calgary and Edmonton international airports has been remarkable and mirrors western Canada's economic growth.
The increase at the Toronto International Airport was also slightly higher than the national average. Air passenger traffic did not increase as quickly in Montreal mostly because of slower economic growth. However, traffic in Mirabel should increase for the following reasons. First, Mr. Speaker, it should be noted that the commitment of the minister concerning Mirabel is unquestionable.
The hon. member is well aware of the ongoing study on the various options to restore traffic between Dorval and Mirabel. When the many factors involved, and especially the costs, have been analysed, a decision will be made. For the moment, I would simply like to give a short list of the programs to be implemented to promote the development of Mirabel.
-The Action Mirabel group which has already succeeded in promoting the airport as a freight centre open 24 hours a day and as a favourite location for trade exhibitions and symposiums.
-Action Mirabel has also worked on the question of access to truckers from the United States.
-The very recent installation of a free transit zone by the Widex Company.
-A proposal to eliminate what is called the "Last Stop Provision" in landing charges at Canadian airports. This would benefit mostly Mirabel.
-The establishment of a Crown corporation to resell the land adjacent to Mirabel.
I could go on, but 1 would simply like to assure the hon. member that the future of Mirabel is a priority for the minister.

subtopic: GRAIN-CHANGE IN POLICY ON TIMING OF ANNOUNCEMENT
GRAIN-CHANGE IN POLICY ON TIMING OF ANNOUNCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this adjournment debate as a result of a question and the response by the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, the assistant to the Minister of Transport.
On March 18 Senator Argue made a statement in the other place regarding the seeding plan producers in Canada should
March 23, 1981

adopt for the coming year. He stated that increases should be in the neighbourhood of 10 per cent for all grains, for barley, and oats. He said durum should remain the same and wheat should be increased by 10 per cent.
The problem arises from the statement by the senator, and the answer given by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in this House. He said that in week 33 of the shipping season, which was last week, there was a scarcity of ocean ships arriving at ports enabling them to loan out of the terminals. That brought the space available in the Vancouver terminals to the lowest level in several years. There was only 49,820 tons of available space in Vancouver.
The assistant to the Minister of Transport made a statement in which he asked producers to increase their production by 10 per cent, without giving them any assurance that they would be able to deliver that grain to market. This also pertains to week 33. We are signalling a warning to the producers and the government that there is a problem building. There are 7,601 loaded cars heading west, compared to last week's total of 7,200 cars, and last year's average of 5,000 cars. I know some people would feel it is progress to have increased loads going west, but when they arrive in the yards we will find there will not be room for them, since last week in the yards there were 14,434 cars in ports to be unloaded.
At the present time there is loading for 11 vessels berthing in Vancouver. Last week there were four vessels loading; there are no ships waiting, according to the information I have. That means when these 7,601 cars arrive in Vancouver there will not be adequate space for them in the terminals. We would like the minister to explain to the farmers in western Canada, who will be putting their crops in within the next six weeks, how they will move their product to market if this situation continues.
1 would also like to take issue with the statement made by the assistant to the minister in the other place in which he stated he was not announcing initial payments this year because last year he announced them too soon. As I mentioned to the Minister of Transport in the House on March 20, it was not that the payments were announced too soon, it was that the statements were inaccurate when they were announced. If you will recall, Mr. Speaker, late in March the minister announced initial payments, readjusted those payments in July and again made a mistake either through incompetence or lack of information. I must say I doubt it was the latter, as at no time since 1971, when this practice was established by the minister's predecessor, the Hon. Otto Lang, was the error so great or the discrepancy so large between the initial payments and the actual interim payments. This practice was established in order that farmers and producers of western Canada would have adequate information in respect of pricing, and thereby have a management tool at their disposal. The present minister would be the only minister since 1971 who would not have that information available to him.
I would like to quote a statement by the Minister of Transport as reported in Hansard for March 20.
Adjournment Debate
He said:
I said the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board did not give the initial prices. He said, however, that he expected the prices to be strong, to remain as they are now, which is an indication of his view on prices.
However, I looked very carefully at Senate Hansard for March 18, when the assistant to the Minister of Transport bootlegged an announcement into the Senate relating to seeding intentions. He stated that:
Last spring I recommended certain initial payments, and 1 got into trouble because I was too careful, too conservative.
He spoke further, but I do not find anything in this statement of the assistant to the Minister of Transport in the other place which would indicate that he expects prices to remain strong and firm.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will be able to add additional light as to why the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board has not followed the practice set by his predecessors since 1971, including the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), who had the same information, the same board, the same commissioners, and the same officials as this minister.
I would again say I do not believe this was done through misinformation. I suspect it is perhaps because the present minister, the assistant to the Minister of Transport, lacks the clout in cabinet to obtain a commitment from this government to guarantee initial payments at a level at which they should be guaranteed; we are aware that the federal government is responsible for any shortfall. I take it that the cabinet does not have a great deal more faith in the assistant to the Minister of Transport in the other place, in his judgment call for the initial pricing of grain, than do the farmers of western Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member raises the question of why this year's pre-seeding report from the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board does not contain an indication of initial price levels for the 1981-82 crop year.
As my hon. friend has noted, this has been the practice since 1971, when it was instituted by Otto Lang, to give farmers a reasonably accurate picture of what to expect in the way of grain prices. That system, by and large, worked well in an environment of stable prices. Last year, it did not work so well. In fact, I remember several complaints from the hon. member that the initial prices were misleading in view of the trend in international prices.
On May 14, he asked the minister in the House about the fact that initial prices were below the previous year's adjusted prices. His colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) brought the subject up again on May 30; and on July 7, the member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) said, and I quote:
In view of the world price for grain today, there is no justification for lowering the initial price.

March 23, 1981
Adjournment Debate
This lowering is in relation to the previously adjusted price. Indeed, the initial prices have since been adjusted not once, but twice, to reflect the very healthy world prices.
My hon. friend obviously recognized that in a highly volatile market, such as the present one, an initial price announced in March is, in fact, not very meaningful. This year, the Minister of State indicated that initial price levels would be set at the beginning of the crop year, as was done before 1971. To give some indication to farmers, however, the minister continued this practice of recommending seeded acreages, most of which are well in excess of last year's. This, at least, will give the farmer some confidence until July when a more meaningful initial price can be announced.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR CODE-PROTECTION OF URANIUM MINERS
CANADA LABOUR CODE-PROTECTION OF URANIUM MINERS
speechtext:
I would like to address my remarks to the subject matter of my question of January 28 of this year which related to the lack of safety provisions in the Canada Labour Code or in any other legislation pertaining to uranium miners at Elliot Lake and elsewhere across Canada. During my question, I said that uranium miners in Elliot Lake and throughout Canada have now been left surrounded and jeopardized by a jurisdictional no man's land which leaves them entirely without protection from the very real and hazardous dangers of their industry. I asked the minister if action was being taken, as promised by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) in reply to an earlier question from the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) on December 16,
1980.	The minister's response was, in part, as reported at page 6647 of Hansard:
1 might say that submissions were made by the steelworkers requesting that joint safety and health committees be established at the two largest uranium mines, Denison and Rio Algom at Elliot Lake. They were accordingly ordered to be established at these two locations in an order dated April 14. As of this date they are not yet in operation, due to the refusal of the steelworkers to nominate labour members to these committees.
The minister added that he wanted to say that I, as the member for Kootenay West, would do a great service if 1 would pass back to my friends, the steelworkers at Elliot Lake, the message that miners there are as well-protected by safety regulations as those in any mine in Canada. To be generous, Mr. Speaker, people all across Canada who are involved in mining know that that statement is not correct. Anyone involved in mining and anyone in the labour movement knows that that is not correct.
Along similar lines, an editorial in the Sault Star on Monday, February 2, 1981, echoed the minister's words when he responded to my question on January 28. Mr. Homer Seguin, the staff representative of the United Steelworkers of America, whose office is at Elliot Lake, wrote a letter to the newspaper which is basically a reply to the comments the minister made when answering my question on January 28. The letter reads as follows:
Let me briefly acquaint you with some of them.
-The government, provincial and federal has over the years, said uranium workers are well protected.
-From 1955 to 1978 the government said the Ontario mining act applied to uranium workers in Ontario. This act did not even mention radiation and had many other shortcomings, however,
-On December 6, 1978, the federal Minister of Labour announced in the House that the Ontario mining act didn't really apply, but, that Part IV of the Canada Labour Code does, contrary to former belief. In passing, it is interesting to note that the Canada Labour Code had no specific provisions for mining. Indeed, there was no expertise nor inspectors in the field. But, the fed's said we were well protected once again.
-Next, the federal government acknowledge (after considerable pressure from the Union) that we were in fact left without real protections, but they would rectify this inadequacy.
-In August 1979, the fed's adopted the old Ontario mining act by reference. Obviously, this was intended to shut us up since it is the same act that was said to apply (but really didn't) since 1955. It's interesting to note that two months later Ontario adopted Bill 70 and discarded the old mining act as obsolete, but not for uranium workers. Ironically, the new Ontario legislation resulted in large part from developments following a three-week safety and health strike in Elliot Lake in 1974. Again, the government said we were well protected.
-Next. Following more pressure, the fed's agreed there was inadequate protection and in May 1980, adopted the Ontario act by reference into its regulations. We were told face to face by Mines Minister Judy Erola that all of the Ontario Act applied. We expressed doubts about the legality of adopting regulations which conflicted with an act but were assured it applied.
-Next, as we attempted to utilize provisions of the Ontario Act, we were told the Ontario Act didn't all apply. For example. The right to refuse unsafe work was not as contained in the Ontario Act, nor was the rights of our safety and health committeemen nor was the composition of our safety and health committees or their protected earnings, etc.
-In support of our contention that our concerns are legitimate you should know that despite acknowledged violations of existing safety legislation (said to apply) not one charge has ever been laid by Labour Canada or the Atomic Energy Control Board involving the Elliot Lake uranium operations.
-we cannot and will not live in a jungle of jurisdictional confusion and unclear legislative protection. This has already killed hundreds of our members.
In support of the United Steelworkers of America position ... I would refer you to the latest government committee report which investigated this whole area of concern.
The all party provincial "Select Committee of Hydro Affairs" issued its final report December 1980 on "Mining, Milling and Refining of Uranium in Ontario." This committee held many meetings, conducted hearings, and investigations for months and generally supports our Union's position.
-you will understand our continuing concern by reading on pages 12 and 13 of the select committee's report their legal opinion as to what protection we really have.
The letter quotes from the committee proceedings as follows:
The committee considers that there is a very real possibility that the government of Canada has not met the technical requirement of the Statutory Instruments Act and that as a result, Ontario's uranium mine workers are operating wholly without the legal protection they are entitled to and have been assured they have.
And finally	comment that the union has refused to name safety and
health committees is ridiculous.
We have told the government agencies and representatives time and time again that our safety and health committees are in place, ready and willing to be legitimised as provided in the Ontario Act. The government has refused. We ask-if the fed's adopted the Ontario Act, then why does it not apply?
There is an old saying that it takes a big man to express honest opinions but it takes a bigger one to acknowledge he was wrong.
March 23, 1981

I would ask the parliamentary secretary, in the absence of the minister this evening, to finally acknowledge that the government is wrong, that the miners at Elliot Lake are in a jurisdictional no man's land. Let us get on, let us work together to attempt to resolve that problem and save the lives of those people working in the uranium industry in the province of Ontario as well as right across Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might point out by way of information that both the parliamentary secretary and the minister are feeling a little under the weather tonight and they asked me, as a former parliamentary secretary to a minister of labour, to read the answer, with your permission, Sir.
With regard to the occupational safety and health protection for uranium miners at Elliot Lake, the federal government's involvement in the Ontario mining industry, as it relates to safety arrangements and practices, is limited to uranium mines and uranium plants which are licensed by the Atomic Energy Control Board. Until October, 1978, the Canada Labour Code, Part IV, which pertains to occupational safety and health was not applied to workers in the uranium mining industry because it is "subject to any other act or regulations," including the Atomic Energy Control Act and the regulations thereunder.
Protection for workers prior to 1978 derived from the requirements of the licence issued by the Atomic Energy Control Board to enterprises in the nuclear field. These licences required such enterprises to conform with the laws of the province in which they were located. This meant that in Ontario workers in uranium mines and processing plants were protected by Ontario's occupational safety and health law
Adjournment Debate
regulations. This arrangement pertained, as mentioned, until the autumn of 1978 when, in response to a letter from the United Steel Workers about jurisdiction, the Atomic Energy Control Board referred the question to the Department of Justice for consideration. The federal justice department at that time gave the opinion that since the AECB had not issued regulations governing occupational safety and health, and since Part IV of the Canada Labour Code was subject only to other acts and regulations, then Part IV applied to uranium mining and processing operations.
The Code does not cover radiation because there are existing AECB regulations respecting radiation and mixed radiation-dust hazards.
Arrangements were worked out with Ontario to reference its occupational safety and health laws by regulation under the Canada Labour Code making them, for purposes of uranium mining, federal laws and thereby designating provincial safety officers as federal safety officers. These arrangements permitted the continuation of the provincial machinery for administering conventional occupational safety and health in uranium mines. Thus, provincial enforcement carried on without significant changes.
On July 11, 1979, and again on April 10, 1980, submissions were made to the ministers of labour by the United Steelworkers Union, requesting that joint safety and health committees be established at the two largest uranium mines, namely, Denison and Rio Algom. In so far as the validity of the referencing of the Ontario occupational health and safety act is concerned, this is a question within the competence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), and as far as this justice department is concerned it says that it is okay and that we must take the word of the law officers of Canada.
